5.0.0.en: 1 My son, attend unto my wisdom, and bow your ear to my understanding: 2 That you may regard discretion, and that your lips may keep knowledge.

5.0.1.en: Every person has two ears in his depths that listen to one voice or another; whoever does not listen with his ears to the voice of wisdom will inevitably listen to strange voices such as the voice of the deceiving adulteress. Therefore, before warning us against this destructive voice, he presents to us the wise, constructive, fatherly voice.

5.0.2.en: The wise man repeats this call so that the believer may listen and incline his ears, as well as his heart, to the voice of his spiritual father, and keep discretion, and gain a knowledge that his lips speak.

5.0.4.en: Bow your ear to my understanding, that you may regard discretion, and that your lips may keep knowledge” [1-2].

5.0.5.en: He calls us to enjoy the living spiritual experiences which the spiritual father lives in the Lord.

5.0.6.en: St. John Cassian spoke, in the fourth book of the “Institutes,” in chapters 9 and 10, about the obligation of novices in monasticism not to rely on their own discernment, and not to hide any of their thoughts from the experienced elder who looks after them. In this way Satan cannot destroy the novice, unless he seduces him by pride and the concealment of his thoughts. The obedience of novice monks should be complete, so that they cannot leave their cells, nor go to attend to their natural needs, without permission. They obey with confidence and certainty and without hesitation as though the command came from heaven.

5.0.7.en: * Whoever has a good mind, and in humility with longing imitates sincerely what he sees, whether through teaching or by following what he sees in the Fathers, instead of being occupied with argument, in this way the knowledge of everything is established in him by practical experience. But those who begin their learning with argument will not enter into the goal of truth... Therefore our enemy (Satan) easily drives them far from the knowledge of the Fathers, until the beneficial and useful matters seem to them unnecessary, even harmful. In this way the cunning enemy plays shrewdly, making them hold stubbornly to their own opinion, convinced that what fills their unclean minds of errors is good, true and holy.

5.0.8.en: Abba Piamun — * It is written: “My son, attend unto my wisdom, bow your ear to my prudence, that your thoughts may be kept” [1]. For truly there is nothing like the heart that tries to flee (from wisdom), which fails us when it slips away with evil thoughts. Therefore the psalmist says: “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps 40:12).

5.0.10.en: The wise man asks his spiritual son to listen, and also asks him to incline his ear to his understanding. If listening indicates the desire to learn and readiness to obey, then the inclining of the inner ear indicates the secret, hidden relationship, for whoever inclines his ear to hear the whispers of another declares his longing to hear private, unannounced words. Together with his ear, a person offers his heart and all his feelings and senses.

5.0.11.en: The wise man used the expression “bow your ear to my understanding,” perhaps drawing on his father, who loved to commune with God, saying: “Incline Your ear unto me” (Ps 17:6). For the Father inclined His ear to humanity by the descent of His Son to us, speaking with us and we with Him as in a secret personal relationship, which the heart hears and the soul responds to with all its hidden energies.

5.0.12.en: So that we may not listen to the voice of the adulteress woman or deceiving sin, let us incline our ear to our heavenly Beloved, saying: “The voice of my beloved! Behold, he leaps upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” (Song 2:8).

5.0.13.en: St. Clement of Alexandria sees in verse 2, “that you may regard discretion, and that your lips may keep knowledge,” a revelation of the Christian view of culture or secular knowledge, for he says:

5.0.14.en: * He advises us indeed to use secular culture, but not to linger and spend (long) time in it. For what is given to every generation in a beneficial way and at suitable times is an elementary training for the word of the Lord. For indeed, some who fell into the snares of the handmaids despised their accompanying philosophy, and grew old. Some fell through music, others through mathematics, others through grammar, and the majority through rhetoric.

5.0.15.en: St. Clement of Alexandria — The prophet Malachi used the expression “keeping knowledge with the lips,” saying: “For the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts” (Mal 2:7). It is as though the mouth of the living believer becomes like a treasury of knowledge under the guard of wise lips, which bring out of these treasures as needed and in the measure fitting for the edification of souls.

5.1.0.en: 3 For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil: 4 But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword. 5 Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell. 6 Lest she should ponder the path of life, her steps sway, and she does not perceive it. 7 Hear me now therefore, O you children, and depart not from the words of my mouth. 8 Remove your way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house: 9 Lest you give your bloom unto others, and your years unto the cruel: 10 Lest strangers be filled with your strength; and your labors be in the house of a stranger; 11 And you mourn at the last, when your flesh and your body are consumed, 12 And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof! 13 And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined my ear to them that instructed me! 14 Were it not for a little, I would have been in all evil in the midst of the company and congregation.

5.1.1.en: If the lips of the believer who listens to the voice of wisdom keep knowledge, then from the lips of the dissolute woman flow sweet words, soft as oil.

5.1.2.en: “For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil.

5.1.3.en: But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword” [3-4].

5.1.4.en: We have already spoken in this book about the strange woman, that she means a Gentile adulteress woman, because according to the Law an Israelite woman caught in adultery was stoned. Therefore some wicked women came and dwelt in the midst of Israel. Perhaps it also means the Israelite woman who falls secretly into adultery, for she is counted a stranger and foreign because she has separated herself from the divine covenant and lost her belonging to the holy people.

5.1.5.en: Her words are outwardly sweet as honey, and inwardly exceedingly bitter as wormwood; outwardly soft as oil, and inwardly like a deadly two-edged sword. Some see that the end bitter as wormwood and the two-edged sword are the venereal diseases from which many who fall into adultery suffer. Perhaps God allowed this so that through what befalls the body man may realize the gravity of what befalls the soul. If the world was shaken some years ago by the discovery of the disease of AIDS, which is often transmitted through wrongful bodily relations, humanity will be shaken when many lose their eternity and their heavenly glory and their fellowship with the heavenly ones because of enslavement to unclean bodily lusts.

5.1.6.en: By the lips and the mouth here are often meant the kisses that stir up evil, together with deceitful, passionate words.

5.1.7.en: The wise man looks at the wicked woman with her mouth of soft lips as a dangerous enemy standing holding a two-edged sword. Every pair of lips is like the edge of a sword, wherever the sword is directed it cuts and destroys... such is the mouth of the wicked woman.

5.1.8.en: * One offers this advice: “Do not notice the beauty of the strange woman, and do not meet a woman who is addicted to adultery. For the lips of the adulteress drop honey, which for a time seems soft to your throat, but afterward you find it more bitter than wormwood, and sharper than a two-edged sword. For the adulterous woman does not know how to love but hunts; her kisses are full of poison, and her mouth is a harmful narcotic. If this does not appear at once, she must be avoided all the more, because she conceals this destruction and seals this death and does not allow it to appear at the beginning.

5.1.9.en: St. John Chrysostom — * The features of the adulteress appear acceptable. I know that, for the Scripture says: “The lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb” [3]. For this reason I bear all this labor, that you may not have experience of this honey, for it immediately turns into wormwood. So also the Holy Scripture says: “That which for a time is soft to your throat, but afterward you find it more bitter than wormwood, and sharper than a two-edged sword” [3, 4] [LXX].

5.1.10.en: St. John Chrysostom — * Thus man deprived himself of the fruits of good things and filled (his belly) with the fruit that brings destruction through disobedience.

5.1.11.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa — “Her feet go down to death.

5.1.12.en: Her steps take hold on hell.

5.2.0.en: Lest we should ponder the path of life, her steps sway, and she does not perceive it” [5-6].

5.2.1.en: He began his description of the adulterous woman with her lips that drop poisoned honey, which she has anointed with the oil of deceit to draw every heart to her. Whoever listens to her goes down to the depths below, “her feet go down to death,” and does not rise to the summits of the high mountains and the firm hills, so he is unable to perceive the voice of his true Beloved. He loses his ability to sing, saying: “The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” (Song 2:8). As St. Gregory of Nyssa comments on this wonderful canticle, saying that the bride, having been awakened in many ways, reached the summit of happiness. Her Bridegroom spoke with her through the Fathers and the prophets, through the mountains and the hills, and now He has come to her Himself to speak with her mouth to mouth and face to face.

5.2.2.en: The danger of the adulterous woman is that her movements sway to the right and to the left, or her steps are unsteady, and so she draws the heart of the one who is joined to her to where he does not know. What is certain is that she takes the one joined to her with her into the kingdom of death.

5.2.3.en: At the beginning she appears as a serpent spreading her venom; her vain lusts form her whole being, her movements and her words, to bring souls down to death sooner or later. Clinging to her hastens the body to destruction and casts the soul into eternal death. She draws the heart and the mind away from contemplating the way of eternal life, not openly but by deceit, and with the passing of time the one who clings to her forgets the day of judgment, so his soul does not long for the crowns of glory, nor does it fear the fire of Gehenna.

5.2.4.en: The apparent marks of the way of sin are: passion, love, sweetness, pleasure, a life of luxury, indulgence and looseness... shining names attractive to man, so he thinks that life without them has no taste, while the true hidden marks of this way are death, hell and eternal destruction. As the wise man places this great day before the eyes of his disciples he says:

5.3.0.en: “Hear me now therefore, O you children, and depart not from my words” [8].

5.3.1.en: * Good, he has begun to fear the day of judgment.

5.3.2.en: May he reform his life by fear, and watch against his enemies, that is, his sins.

5.3.3.en: May he begin to set out toward the inner life again and put to death his members which are upon the earth, as the Apostle says.

5.4.0.en: St. Augustine — “Remove your way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house” [9].

5.4.1.en: The wise man offers us this advice, which is to keep away from the way of sin and not to approach the entrance of its house, lest we fall into its snares.

5.4.2.en: * This advice which the author of Proverbs offers us: “Remove your way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house” [8] concerns the adulteress. I wish to repeat the same thing concerning the love of money. For by entering gradually into it you fall into a sea of madness and cannot get rid of it easily. So you are like one in a storm: you struggle as much as you can, yet you do not easily reach deliverance from it. For after you fall into the evil pit of covetousness you destroy yourself and all that you possess (Acts 8:20).

5.4.3.en: Thus my advice is that we must be on guard from the beginning, and avoid small evils, for great evils come out of these.

5.4.4.en: St. John Chrysostom — “Lest you give your bloom (your honor) unto others, and your years unto the cruel” [9].

5.4.5.en: In the literal sense the wise man warns the person whom sin deceives, especially adultery, lest the husband discover what this fallen man does with his unfaithful wife, and so he loses his honor before him, indeed before the whole community, and is condemned to death, or falls under punishments that embitter his life. Spiritually, what is more serious is that what a person commits is known to heaven, so he loses his place there, and has no portion among the heavenly ones and the saints. He loses his splendor, which it was fitting for him to possess through his constant meeting with God and his fellowship with the heavenly ones, and so he plunges with the devil and his hosts into humiliation, shame and dishonor.

5.4.6.en: When a person is negligent with himself and approaches sin or stands beside its door, he loses his self-respect and forgets his dignity in the Lord, and hands over the rest of his life to the enemy of good. Sin, especially adultery, often seems gentle and kind, but it subjects us to a violent, tyrannical master, and destroys the soul and its true dignity.

5.4.7.en: * Who are strangers to us but the perishing spirits who have been separated from the company of the heavenly ones? And what is our dignity but that, although we are bodies of clay, we were created in the image and likeness of our Maker?! Or who is cruel but the apostate angel who inflicted upon himself the pain of death through pride, and has not ceased to bring death upon the human race although he himself is lost?! Therefore he who was created in the image and likeness of God and devoted the seasons of his life to the pleasures of the perishing spirits gives his dignity to strangers.

5.4.9.en: “Lest strangers be filled with your strength; and your labors be in the house of a stranger.

5.5.0.en: And you mourn at the last, when your flesh and your body are consumed” [10-11].

5.5.1.en: Evil is like a violent storm that blows and shatters everything. When a person commits sin, especially adultery, he thinks he is enjoying a kind of satisfaction instead of deprivation, not knowing that he is handing over his strength to the enemy of good, and handing over all he owns to a stranger’s house, not only in the spiritual aspect but even in material matters, since his life often ends in bitterness. He loses much of his possessions and loses the health of his body.

5.5.2.en: Perhaps he means here that when the matter of the adulterer is discovered he is obliged to provide for the woman with whom he fell into adultery, and for the child born of her, for life; in this way strangers are filled with his strength and his labor is in a stranger’s house.

5.5.3.en: “And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof! And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined my ear to them that instructed me!

5.6.0.en: Were it not for a little, I would have been in all evil in the midst of the company and congregation” [12-14].

5.6.1.en: The matter is not, as some think, a field for amusement, but it is truly dangerous, for what a man sows, that he also reaps. Perhaps we now see how societies groan from the fruits of the dissoluteness that was sown in the hearts of the new generations, and so reaped bitterness and destruction.

5.6.2.en: According to the Mosaic Law the adulterer is exposed to stoning to death (Deut 22:22), but what is more serious is that a person loses eternal life.

5.6.3.en: Although he is in the midst of the company and congregation, that is, in the midst of the Church of the Old Testament or the New Testament, he has deprived himself of her peace and joy, and has isolated himself from her by not listening to the voice of his spiritual father, his guide and teacher. He refused chastening and rebuke, and so lost his membership in the Church even if he carries it outwardly.

5.6.4.en: * Whoever relies on his own opinion, even if he is a saint, is deceived, and the danger of his deception is greater than the danger of the beginner who has handed his guidance into the hand of another. The former is like a ship’s captain who threw himself into a boat without sail or oar in the middle of the sea, relying on his skill and the art of his management. The latter, that is, the beginner, is like one who has no experience in sea travel, and asks a skilled sailor to take him aboard his ship, which is furnished with all its necessities and needs.

5.6.5.en: Let none of you be deceived and flee from the gentle yoke of obedience, resolved to hold fast to his own opinion in spiritual matters such as fasting and prayer and other signs of faith and asceticism, thinking that by this he is saved!!

5.6.6.en: John Chrysostom — * Obedience... is the denial of the self, the death of the will, the grave of passion, the resurrection of humility...

5.6.7.en: Obedience is the death of the members of the body and of the passion of the soul, and that is with pain for the beginner, at one time with pain and at another without pain for the intermediate, while the perfect feels no pain unless he does something according to the passion of his soul...

5.6.8.en: So those who wish to bear the yoke of Christ on their necks, and place their burdens on the necks of others (their fathers or spiritual guides), their way is to reject their own passions and do what they see to be in accord with the will of God.

5.6.9.en: * Without a guide there is no safety. From obedience comes humility, and from humility comes healing from the passions. For it is written that in our humility the Lord remembered us and delivered us from our enemies.

5.6.10.en: John Chrysostom — * How happy is he who puts his will to death and leaves the management of his soul to the one whom God has given him as father and teacher, for his place will be at the right hand of Jesus Christ the Crucified.

5.6.11.en: * He who obeys his father once and disobeys him another time, obeys him in one thing and disobeys him in another, is at one time building and at another time tearing down, and so his labor is in vain.

5.6.12.en: * He who obeys his spiritual father at one time and disobeys him at another is like one who at one time puts good water on his sick eyes, and at another time puts hot lime on them.

5.6.13.en: The Fathers said that singing the Psalms is a weapon, prayer is a safeguard, pure tears are a washing, and virtuous obedience is a testimony, so without confession and obedience sinners are not saved.

5.6.14.en: * The way of obedience is the shortest of paths, though it is the most difficult. And there is only one way in which, whenever we walk, we go astray: it is what we call “reliance on the self and on our own personal will.”

5.6.15.en: * Obedience is a plea before God. If you are asked by Him: Why did you do this? You answer Him: “You, O Lord, commanded obedience, and I did what You commanded,” and so you answer Him and are justified.

5.6.16.en: Traveling on this ship is safe from shipwreck. A man travels while he sleeps, just as a man travels in a ship asleep and is not obliged to manage it, because its manager is present. Such is the state of the man who walks under obedience: he travels toward heaven and perfection while he sleeps, without toil or thought of what he ought to do. For the superiors are the managers of this ship and the ones who keep watch for him. I swear that it is no light matter but is very great. For man crosses the sea of this world upon the arm and forearm of another!! This is the great grace which God does with the one who walks under obedience.

5.7.0.en: 15 Drink waters out of your own cistern, and running waters out of your own well. 16 Let not your fountains overflow outward, channels of water in the streets. 17 Let them be only your own, and not strangers’ with you. 18 Let your fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of your youth, 19 The loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy you at all times; and be ravished always with her love. 20 And why will you, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger? 21 For the ways of man are before the eyes of the Lord, and He weighs all his paths.

5.7.1.en: “Drink waters out of your own cistern, and running waters out of your own well” [15].

5.7.2.en: In ancient times the owners of houses and fields prized the wells they dug and the cistern they excavated as exceedingly special and precious possessions (2 Kgs 18:31; Jer 38:6).

5.7.3.en: Here he points to faithfulness in married life, where the two spouses are joined together in the Lord, so each of them drinks from his own cistern, where he sees the waters of love in the heart of the other party, counting it his cistern and his deep well and his fountain.

5.7.4.en: The wise man here presents a lofty and holy view of conjugal love, at a time when speaking of the bodily relations between spouses was considered shameful and disgraceful. Here he declares that marriage is sanctified by God, so each of the spouses feels esteem for the other and sanctity in the passionate feelings, and even for his own body and the body of the other. The Apostle Peter speaks to husbands, saying: “Giving honor unto them as being heirs together with you of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered” (1 Pet 3:7).

5.7.5.en: Whoever seeks passion or lustful love, or hands over his body to one other than (his wife or her husband), lets his fountain overflow outward and squanders his waters in the streets; he loses what is his, since he hands the waters of his love over to a stranger.

5.7.6.en: It is noticed that the word “well” or “cistern” in Hebrew is in the singular, as though the wise Solomon, who for political reasons fell into polygamy, makes clear here the attachment of a person to one wife, whom he regards as his one fountain, as she regards her husband as her one fountain... God created Eve alone for Adam, and he is to be hers.

5.7.7.en: * Isaiah says: “Ho, every one who thirsts, come to the waters” (Isa 55:1). And Solomon urges us: “Drink waters out of your own vessel”...

5.7.8.en: The philosopher Plato, who learned from the Hebrews, commands husbands not to drink or take water from others, but to dig first in their own land (attachment to the wife alone), which is said to be virgin land.

5.7.9.en: St. Clement of Alexandria — * If you look in impurity, desiring your neighbor’s wife, your portion will be with the adulterers... Leave your fountain to yourself and drink water from your own well. Let your fountains be yours alone and let no other drink with you. Seek the purity of your body as you ask it of the other party. For as you do not want the wife of your youth to be defiled with another man, do not defile yourself with another woman, the wife of another man.

5.7.10.en: Mar Ephrem the Syrian — * Let the fountain of your waters (your wife) be yours alone and not strangers’ with you... Then do not concern yourself with a foreign river (another woman), nor with delighting other women more than your wife. Lest, if you are carried off to another place, you practice the law of uncleanness with the other party as well.

5.7.11.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus — And the inner fountain is the overflow of divine love which the Holy Spirit causes to burst forth in us.

5.7.12.en: * Good, then, are these waters, which are the grace of the Spirit.

5.7.13.en: Who will give me this fountain for my breast?

5.7.14.en: Let it spring up within me, let Him who gives eternal life overflow upon me.

5.7.15.en: Let this fountain overflow upon me and not outside of me. For Wisdom says: “Drink waters out of your own cistern, and running waters out of your own well; let not your fountains overflow into the streets.”

5.7.16.en: How shall I keep this water so that it does not overflow and run far away?

5.7.17.en: How shall I keep the vessel so that the crack of sin does not strike it, and the waters of eternal life leak out of it?

5.7.18.en: Teach us, O Lord! Teach us as You taught Your disciples, saying: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal” (Mt 6:19).

5.7.19.en: St. Ambrose — If the wise man speaks here of the purity of the married, his speech also applies to the purity of teaching. The teacher who preaches what others say without having experienced it in his practical life does not drink from the waters of his cistern, nor enjoy the waters of his well. It is fitting for us to drink from the fountains of our inner hearts, where the Holy Spirit overflows with His waters in them, so we are watered and overflow upon others.

5.7.20.en: * Open the porch of your heart to the Word of God, who says to you: “Open your mouth and I will fill it!”

5.7.21.en: St. Ambrose — * All who do not love God are strangers and antichrists. Though they come to the churches, they cannot be counted among the children of God, and the fountain of life does not belong to them.

5.7.22.en: That a man be baptized is possible even for the wicked; that a man prophesy is possible for the wicked!

5.7.23.en: St. Augustine — “Let not your fountains overflow outward, channels of water in the streets.

5.8.0.en: Let them be only your own, and not strangers’ with you” [16-17].

5.8.1.en: What does he mean by the one who overflows with his waters outward and casts the channels of water into the streets? He is that fool who does not care about the value of water in remote regions, and so squanders it by sprinkling it in the streets.

5.8.2.en: Some see here a picture of some men in ancient times who did not sanctify family life, so the man was not content with one wife to care for with their children, but all that occupied him was satisfying his lusts with more than one wife, and pleasing them all by having children from him... so that sometimes he does not know the names of his children because of their great number, and therefore does not offer them the spirit of fatherhood or care for their upbringing and salvation.

5.8.3.en: Perhaps he means that whoever drinks from the outside fountain, that is, from other than his wife (or her husband), pushes the other party to give himself or herself over to adultery. While the man drinks from a fountain that is not his, he loses his own fountain (his wife), who gives her feelings and perhaps her body to another. In this way he sins against himself and against his life partner.

5.8.4.en: * When anyone diverts the energy of his thoughts to evil, he has squandered the overflow of waters upon strangers.

5.8.5.en: As long as we water the path of our life, in which thorns spread, with the waters of evil thoughts, the good plants dry up and perish, because their roots are not refreshed by the moisture of good thoughts.

5.9.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa — “Let your fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of your youth” [18].

5.10.0.en: “The loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy you at all times; and be ravished always with her love” [19].

5.10.1.en: * The Word of God is living, and the soul that receives Him is living. This kind of water overflows from God, for the Fountain Himself says: “For I proceeded forth and came from God” (Jn 8:42). The bride has an overflow of water within the well of her soul, so she becomes a treasury for this living water that flows from Lebanon (Song 4:15).

5.10.2.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa — Let the spouses walk in a spirit of simplicity with love, for as the infant is satisfied from his mother’s breasts, so the spouses are satisfied from their mutual love.

5.10.3.en: The likening of the wife to the loving hind and the delighting roe points to the purity of love and the swiftness of response between them. The hind signifies purity of body, and the delighting roe swiftness of movement.

5.10.4.en: The wise Solomon used similar words in the Song of Songs (Song 2:9, 17; 4:5; 7:3).

5.11.0.en: “And why will you, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?” [20].

5.11.1.en: The verb here in the original means that a person wanders or goes astray until he becomes a captive. So it is with one who falls into the snares of an adulteress (a stranger) or the wife of another man. He thinks she is attached to him and loves him, and does not know that she is taking him captive in the cords of sin that destroy freedom.

5.11.2.en: “For the ways of man are before the eyes of the Lord, and He weighs all his paths.

5.11.3.en: His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be held with the cords of his sin.

5.11.4.en: He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall act recklessly” [21-23].

5.11.5.en: He asks us for inner and outer purity, so that we are not ravished by a strange woman through our hidden glances or thought, and do not embrace a stranger by practical conduct. For God looks at man and knows his hidden secrets and his outward actions. As the Apostle says: “Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in His sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do” (Heb 4:13).

5.11.6.en: Whoever falls into sin binds himself with its cords, and drinks from its cup, and eats its deadly fruits. For sin carries its wages within itself, where it enslaves him, humiliates him and destroys him.

5.11.7.en: * You harm no one; rather every man is bound by the cords of his sin. (See Ps 7:15-16; 57:6).

5.11.8.en: St. Augustine — * “Let them fall into the snare (which they set)... a grave recompense, there is no justice greater than this! They hid a snare so that I would not know it, so that the snare which they do not know might catch them... The wicked is bound by the cords of his sin, therefore the wicked are deceived by that with which they wish to deceive others. Then harm comes upon them when they wish harm to others. Therefore it is said: “Let the net that they hid catch them, and let them fall into their own snare.”

5.11.9.en: He is like one who prepares a cup of poison for another, and forgets that he will drink from it himself, or one who digs a pit to make his enemy fall into it in the darkness, forgetting that he himself will first walk on the road in which he dug and fall...

5.11.10.en: St. Augustine — * The very pleasures we enjoy become torment to us, and the delights and pleasures of the flesh turn into tormentors of the one who produced them.

5.12.0.en: 22 His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be held with the cords of his sin. 23 He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall act recklessly.

5.12.1.en: He concludes his speech here with the end of the reckless “fool” who does not control himself. It is noticed that the word “self-control” occurs 42 times in this book, and the word “fool” is repeated 40 times; so those who do not control themselves live in a spirit of folly and ignorance, and those who walk in folly lose their control of themselves.

5.12.2.en: The summary of this chapter is that whoever bows himself before bodily lusts loses his self-control and lives in stupidity.

5.12.3.en: The divine teaching concerning bodily relations:

5.12.4.en: This chapter affirms that every relationship into which a young man falls before his marriage has its effect on his home in the future; for purity keeps a man in his home to drink from his good fountain. Wrongful relationships destroy the young man’s inner peace and rob him of the sanctity of the view of married life, especially in bodily relations, so he drinks bitterness and loses the sweetness of family life.

5.12.5.en: Let me incline my ear to Your voice,
